questions.q: What is the primary source of lymph in the human body, and how does it enter the lymphatic system?
questions.a: Lymph originates as interstitial fluid (tissue fluid) that forms when water and small water-soluble substances filter out of blood capillaries into tissue spaces. This fluid enters the lymphatic capillaries to become lymph. A wrong answer (e.g., "lymph is secreted by lymph nodes" or "lymph comes directly from arteries") reveals a misconception that lymph is actively produced by lymphatic organs rather than being a filtrate of blood plasma.

questions.q: Why is lymph described as a "colourless fluid" despite being derived from blood, which is red?
questions.a: Lymph is colourless because it lacks erythrocytes (RBCs) and haemoglobin; during capillary filtration, the larger formed elements (RBCs, platelets, most proteins) are retained in the blood vessels. A wrong answer (e.g., "lymph loses its colour in lymph nodes") indicates confusion between filtration and cellular processing, and a lack of understanding of the size-based selectivity of capillary endothelium.

questions.q: A patient has a blockage in the thoracic duct. Predict the consequences on (a) fluid balance in the left leg and (b) fat absorption from the intestine.
questions.a: (a) The left leg drains into the thoracic duct; blockage would cause lymph accumulation (lymphedema) in the left leg and left side of the body. (b) The thoracic duct receives chyle (fat-rich lymph) from the intestinal lacteals via the cisterna chyli; blockage would impair fat absorption, leading to malnutrition and steatorrhea. A wrong answer shows inability to integrate anatomical drainage patterns with physiological functions.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the composition of lymph and blood plasma. Explain how the differences relate to their respective functions.
questions.a: Lymph has similar mineral distribution and water content as plasma but lower protein concentration (especially albumin) and lacks RBCs and platelets; it contains lymphocytes. These differences exist because capillary endothelium filters out large proteins and cells. Lymph's low protein content reduces oncotic pressure, facilitating fluid return; lymphocytes enable immune surveillance. A wrong answer that states "lymph has same proteins as plasma" misses the filtration concept and its functional significance.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The lymphatic system is a closed circulatory system parallel to the blood vascular system." Justify your answer.
questions.a: The statement is false. The lymphatic system is a one-way (open) system: it begins blindly in tissues as lymphatic capillaries, has no pump (heart), and drains into veins. Blood vascular system is closed with a pump (heart) and continuous circuit. A wrong evaluation (calling it closed) reveals confusion between "parallel" and "closed", and overlooks the structural and functional differences in fluid propulsion.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to demonstrate that lymph flows only in one direction (towards the heart) in a lymphatic vessel. Mention the principle used.
questions.a: Use a live frog's webbed foot (or transparent lymphatic vessel in a suitable animal model) under a microscope. Inject a tiny dye particle into a lymphatic capillary and observe its movement; it moves only towards larger vessels and ultimately towards the subclavian vein. Alternatively, compress a lymphatic vessel distal to a valve and observe that flow stops, but proximal compression does not reverse flow. Principle: presence of valves in lymphatic vessels ensures unidirectional flow. A poor answer (e.g., "measure pressure at two points") fails to address the valvular mechanism and direct observation of flow direction.
